name: Social media detox

lead: A social media detox is a set period of reduced or stopped use of platforms. People take one to see fewer idealised faces and bodies, so there is less appearance comparison and a better self-image.

Experiments link viewing idealised images on social networks with higher body dissatisfaction, which is the reasoning behind the break. Meta-analyses of randomised trials report small and sometimes inconsistent effects on well-being; a 2024 meta-analysis found reduced depression but no significant effect on well-being, life satisfaction or stress, and a 2025 study in Body Image compared detox strategies for body image and well-being.

paras: People limit or abstain from apps for days to weeks, sometimes using blocking tools or app timers, or delete apps from their phone. Researchers measure well-being, depression, body image and problematic use before and after. Some people return with a trimmed, more selective feed.
No physical risks. Some people report increased fear of missing out or social pressure during a detox, and results across studies are mixed.

web.title: Social media and body image - Wikipedia

angle.text: A break from social platforms cuts exposure to idealised faces and bodies, which means less appearance comparison and a better self-image. Trials show small, mixed effects on well-being, and appearance outcomes are not directly studied.

lead: A social media detox, a form of digital detox, is a deliberate break from social media or other devices, ranging from usage limits to complete abstinence for a set period.[1] In appearance terms, the idea is to reduce the constant stream of idealised faces, bodies and edited photos that people compare themselves with, in the hope of feeling more satisfied with how they look and spending the saved time on sleep, training, skincare and other routines.[2]

Research is mixed overall but includes a randomised trial aimed squarely at appearance. A 2025 study in Body Image randomised 175 women aged 17 to 35 to one of three seven-day strategies (an Instagram/TikTok break, a 30-minute daily cap, or a feed cleanse removing appearance-focused content) or to usual use. Appearance satisfaction improved in all three detox groups and not in the control group.[3] More general reviews report small effects on well-being: a 2024 meta-analysis found reduced depression but no significant effect on life satisfaction or stress, and a 2025 meta-analysis of 20 randomised trials found a small positive effect on well-being.[4][5]

Experiments summarised on Wikipedia link exposure to idealised images with body dissatisfaction, with appearance comparison as a key factor, which is the rationale behind detoxes in appearance-related self-improvement discussion.[2]

paras: The chain people describe runs from less exposure to idealised content, to less appearance comparison, to higher appearance satisfaction and body appreciation. The Body Image trial measured exactly these outcomes, including self-objectification, appearance satisfaction, body appreciation and media pressure, over seven days. Appearance satisfaction rose in every detox condition, and it kept rising between day 3 and day 7 in the group that removed appearance-focused content from feeds while still using the apps.[3]

A second route is indirect: a two-week study of 31 young adults who limited use to 30 minutes a day reported improved sleep, stress, life satisfaction and perceived wellness alongside lower problematic smartphone and social media use.[6] Sleep and stress are commonly discussed as affecting skin, energy and training.

Wikipedia's article on social media and body image adds context for why people curate rather than quit: it reports that body and face reshaping apps and filters have been linked to body dysmorphia concerns and to people seeking surgery to resemble filtered images, and that 87 percent of women and 65 percent of men in one survey compared their bodies with images they consume.[2]

Approaches include full abstinence, time limits and app blockers.[1] A survey study of 263 detox-app users examined how personality traits relate to perceptions of those apps.[7] Variants discussed in the research include platform-specific breaks, daily time caps and feed cleaning, in which users unfollow or mute appearance-focused accounts instead of leaving.[3]

Meta-analytic findings are small and inconsistent across reviews.[1][4][5] The 2024 meta-analysis pooled 10 studies and reported a significant reduction in depression, with a standardised mean difference of about -0.29, and no statistically significant effects on life satisfaction or stress.[4] The 2025 meta-analysis of 20 randomised trials and 56 effect sizes found a small positive effect on well-being, with heterogeneity linked to cultural background and, for negative indicators, to intervention length.[5]

Wikipedia notes that detoxes can increase fear of missing out and social pressure, and that critics argue social media provides social capital and that moderation may be preferable to abstinence.[1] A study of relapse predictors examined why people return to use.[8]

A 2025 JAMA Network Open study followed young adults aged 18 to 24 for a two-week baseline of passively monitored use and an optional one-week detox, measuring depression and anxiety symptoms as outcomes, in part because earlier work relied heavily on self-reported use.[9]

A systematic review and meta-analysis examined digital detox interventions and mental health outcomes.[4] A 2025 meta-analysis of randomised trials examined detox and well-being.[5] An exploratory two-week detox study in young adults measured problematic smartphone and social media use and related health outcomes and found improvements in addiction scores, sleep, satisfaction with life, stress and supportive relationships.[6] The 2025 Body Image trial compared three detox approaches for body image and wellbeing: wellbeing improved from baseline to posttest in the daily time-cap group.[3] Experimental reviews on idealised social media images and body dissatisfaction are summarised by Wikipedia, including a review of 43 experiments with 8,637 participants.[2]
